title: The Definite Past Time Trap (Present Perfect vs Simple Past)
frequency: Extremely High (Appears in 80%+ of State Exams)
explanation: Present Perfect ('has/have + V₃') connects a past action to the present moment. Therefore, do not pair Present Perfect with adverbs denoting finished, definite past time (such as yesterday, ago, last week, in 2021). When a finished past time anchor is present, use Simple Past ('V₂'). However, if specifying an action actively in progress at a specific past point ('at 4 PM yesterday'), use Past Continuous ('was/were + V-ing').
incorrectExample: The advocate general has argued the bail application yesterday.
correctExample: The advocate general argued the bail application yesterday.
trapRule: Finished Past Time Adverbs (yesterday, ago, last...) ➔ Simple Past (V₂); Action in progress at past point ➔ Past Continuous.

title: The 'Did + V₂' Redundancy Pitfall (Auxiliary vs. Lexical Verb)
explanation: In Simple Past affirmative clauses, V₂ is the past lexical verb form (no auxiliary verb is present). In negative sentences ('did not') and interrogatives ('Did + Subject...?'), 'did' functions as the auxiliary verb and carries the past inflection. Consequently, the lexical verb MUST remain in its base form (V₁). Using a past form after 'did' creates an erroneous double-past construction.
incorrectExample: The petitioner did not submitted the requisite documents on time.
correctExample: The petitioner did not submit the requisite documents on time.
trapRule: Auxiliary 'did' + Lexical Base Verb (V₁). Never use V₂ after 'did'.

title: The Stative Verb Progressive Distortion
explanation: Certain English verbs express cognitive states, emotions, perceptions, or possession rather than dynamic physical activities. These 'stative verbs' (know, believe, understand, belong, possess, remember) resist continuous/progressive (-ing) aspect under standard usage. Use Simple Present instead. Note that frequency adverbs like 'always' can accompany continuous dynamic verbs to express irritation (e.g., 'He is always interrupting').
incorrectExample: The judicial registrar is knowing the procedural guidelines thoroughly.
correctExample: The judicial registrar knows the procedural guidelines thoroughly.
trapRule: Stative verbs (know, belong, understand, believe, want) take Simple Aspect, NOT Continuous.

title: The 'Since' vs 'For' & Duration Context Trap
explanation:
Learners frequently confuse 'since' and 'for', or assume 'for' invariably forces a continuous tense:
• 'Since' marks a specific starting point in time (since 9 AM, since 2019).
• 'For' marks a duration span (for 3 hours, for 5 years).
• Critical Contextual Rule: Duration does not invariably force Present Perfect Continuous. A completed period in the past takes Simple Past ('He worked in Jaipur for three years'). A period extending to the present takes Present Perfect ('He has worked here for three years') or Present Perfect Continuous for dynamic activity ('He has been working for 3 hours').
incorrectExample: He has been serving in the High Court computer wing since five years.
correctExample: He has been serving in the High Court computer wing for five years.
trapRule: Since = Starting Point | For = Duration Count (Completed period = Simple Past; Period extending to present = Present Perfect / Perf Cont).

title: The 'By + Time' Completion Boundary Trap
explanation: When a sentence contains 'by + future time' (e.g., 'by tomorrow', 'by 6 PM'), it signals that an action will be completed on or before that deadline, typically taking Future Perfect ('will have + V₃') rather than Simple Future ('will complete'). Similarly, 'by + past time' (e.g., 'by 5 PM yesterday') marks completion prior to a past boundary, taking Past Perfect ('had + V₃').
incorrectExample: The system assistant will upload all case records by 6 PM today.
correctExample: The system assistant will have uploaded all case records by 6 PM today.
trapRule: By + Future Time Benchmark ➔ Future Perfect (will have + V₃); By + Past Time Benchmark ➔ Past Perfect (had + V₃).

title: The Isolated Past Perfect Fallacy (Past Reference Point Required)
explanation: Past Perfect ('had + V₃') is not merely an older simple past; it requires a specific past reference point or prior completed context (e.g., 'The team had compiled the dossier by 4 PM yesterday'). An independent single past event without a reference boundary must take Simple Past ('V₂'), not Past Perfect. Advanced multi-clause Sequence of Tenses rules between two past events are systematically mastered in Lesson 02.
incorrectExample: The advocate general had filed the writ petition yesterday.
correctExample: The advocate general filed the writ petition yesterday.
trapRule: Single isolated past event ➔ Simple Past (V₂). Past Perfect ('had + V₃') requires a prior reference boundary (Lesson 02 covers cross-clause sequence).
